intro: This unit follows a thread of tall figures through the Hebrew Bible. Twelve scouts come back from Canaan afraid of the sons of Anak. Og of Bashan has a bed nine cubits long. Goliath steps out from Gath. Behind them all stands a rare word, Nephilim, first used in Genesis 6.

The unit starts from the texts themselves: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Samuel and the Psalms, the Greek Septuagint, a Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel, 1 Enoch, Josephus and clay tablets from Ugarit. Then it asks how researchers read them. Michael Heiser tied the giant clans to Genesis 6 and read Bashan and Hermon as places with a spiritual reputation. Loren Stuckenbruck, George Nickelsburg and others studied the giants and Watchers of 1 Enoch. Other readers see tall warriors, or the bold language of ancient war reports. You will hear each view fairly.

By the end you will be able to trace the giant clans from Numbers to 1 Samuel. You will compare what old manuscripts say about Goliath's height and explain what Rephaim means. You will explain why some scholars link places like Bashan and Hermon with spiritual powers. You will also talk calmly and fairly about the hard questions of the conquest stories.
bigQuestion: What did the biblical writers mean by giants, and why do readers explain them so differently?

timeline.t: Scribes at Ugarit write clay tablets that speak of the rpum and of Rapiu
The city of Ugarit is destroyed, and its tablets lie buried
David rules in Israel, in the Bible's telling (dates are approximate)
King Mesha of Moab sets up a stone boasting of victory over Israel
Jewish scholars begin the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
The Book of the Watchers, the first part of 1 Enoch, is circulating
A scroll of Samuel, 4QSamuel-a, is copied; it gives Goliath four cubits and a span
Josephus writes his Antiquities, also giving Goliath four cubits and a span
The Leningrad Codex is copied, the oldest complete Masoretic Hebrew Bible
Excavations begin at Ras Shamra, the site of ancient Ugarit
Qumran Cave 4 is found, holding thousands of scroll fragments, among them 4QSamuel-a
J. T. Milik publishes the Aramaic fragments of 1 Enoch from Qumran Cave 4

words.d: a rare Hebrew word for a group of very tall people, found only in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33
a people the Bible describes as very tall, named as descendants of a man called Anak
a Hebrew word used for tall clans in Deuteronomy and Joshua, and for the dead in other books
an ancient measure from the elbow to the fingertip, about 18 inches
the standard Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, carefully copied by Jewish scribes called Masoretes
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun by Jewish scholars around 250 BCE
an ancient city on the Syrian coast whose clay tablets shed light on the Hebrew Bible
a fertile region east and northeast of the Sea of Galilee, ruled by Og in the Bible
the tallest mountain in the region, about 9,200 feet; in 1 Enoch, where the Watchers came down
Heiser's term for the biblical idea that places on earth were linked to spiritual powers
the ban: devoting a city and its people to God by destruction, in the conquest stories

test.q: Which two verses are the only places the word Nephilim appears?
test.why: Nephilim appears only in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33.

test.q: What did the scouts say they seemed like beside the sons of Anak?
test.why: In Numbers 13:33 the scouts say they seemed like grasshoppers.

test.q: What did the Ammonites call the tall people of their land?
test.why: Deuteronomy 2:20 says the Ammonites called them Zamzummim; the Moabites used Emim.

test.q: How long was Og's bed, according to Deuteronomy 3:11?
test.why: Deuteronomy 3:11 says nine cubits long and four cubits wide.

test.q: Where does Joshua 11:22 say Anakim remained?
test.why: Joshua 11:22 names the three coastal cities Gaza, Gath and Ashdod.

test.q: What height does the Dead Sea Scroll 4QSamuel-a give Goliath?
test.why: 4QSamuel-a reads four cubits and a span; the Masoretic Text reads six.

test.q: What are the Masoretes known for?
test.why: The Masoretes were Jewish scribes who copied the Hebrew text; the Septuagint is the Greek translation.

test.q: In Psalm 88:10 and Isaiah 26:14, what does rephaim mean?
test.why: In these verses rephaim names those in the realm of the dead.

test.q: What did Michael Heiser argue about the giant clans in The Unseen Realm (2015)?
choices: The Bible links them back to the Nephilim of Genesis 6
They built the pyramids of Egypt
They were invented by the King James translators
test.why: Heiser argued, in The Unseen Realm (2015), that the writers tied the clans to Genesis 6.

test.q: About how high is Mount Hermon?
test.why: Hermon rises about 9,200 feet; Zion is about 2,500 feet.

test.q: In which churches is 1 Enoch part of the Bible?
choices: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
test.why: 1 Enoch is canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

test.q: Why does the tablet KTU 1.108 from Ugarit interest readers of Joshua 12:4?
choices: It names Ashtaroth and Edrei, the cities of Og
It tells the story of David and Goliath
test.why: KTU 1.108 places Rapiu in Ashtaroth and Edrei, where Joshua 12:4 places Og.

test.q: In Psalm 68:15-16, which two mountains are set against each other?
choices: Zion and the Mount of Olives
The mountain of Bashan and Zion
test.why: Psalm 68 pictures Bashan's mountain looking with envy at Zion, the mountain God desired.

test.q: What does the Mesha Stele show about ancient war writing?
choices: A king could claim a total victory that did not happen
War reports were written only in Hebrew
test.why: Mesha boasted that Israel had perished forever, a clear case of hyperbole.

test.q: Which people does the Bible say were spared during the conquest?
test.why: Joshua 6:25 spares Rahab's family, and Joshua 9 tells of the Gibeonites' treaty.

write.prompt: Did the biblical writers mean to link the giant clans to Genesis 6? Cite two or three passages from this unit, such as Numbers 13:33, Deuteronomy 3:11, Joshua 11:22 or 1 Samuel 17:4. Explain what each says, then compare two readings, such as Heiser's thread reading and the hyperbole reading.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you use.
Attribute each view: Heiser argues, Nickelsburg reads, other scholars think, many readers believe.
Compare the readings; you do not need to say who is right.
Use unit terms such as Nephilim, Rephaim and Masoretic Text.
Keep a calm, respectful tone toward every reader.
